To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic blockade of brain monoamine transporters results in specific reductions in the ability of D2, 3- HT1A, and a-adrenergic G-proteins to respond to receptor activation in specific brain regions.

chronic treatment with WF-3, a highly potent biogenic amine uptake blocker, causes a specific reduction in receptor/G-protein signaling, but does not cause receptor downregulation, as determined by receptor binding studies.
long-term blockade of monoamine transporter function produces specific reductions in G-protein coupling for specific receptors, without downregulation of the receptors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of chronic monoamine transport blockade on brain monoamine levels, receptor/G-protein interactions, and behavioral responses.
the effects of chronic monoamine depletion on receptor/G-protein coupling in the brain.
the development of novel, highly potent and selective inhibitors of monoamine transport.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
long-term blockade of monoamine uptake by WF-23 produces specific uncouplings of D2, 2-AR and 5-HT1AR from their respective G-proteins.
long-term blockade of monoamine transporter function produces selective uncoupling of specific monoamine receptors and G-protein complexes in the absence of downregulation of receptor density.
chronic monoamine transporter blockade produces a specific uncoupling effect on G-protein-coupled receptors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
long-term monoamine transporter blockade produces a selective and specific uncoupling between monoamine receptors and G-protein signaling.
chronic elevation of monoamine levels in brain uncouples specific monoamine receptors from G-proteins, but not other receptors, in a region-specific fashion.
chronic blockade of the biogenic amine transporters with WF-23 produces specific and selective uncoupling of G-protein coupled receptors and G-protein signaling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
long-term elevation of monoamine levels in brain can lead to specific changes in receptor/G-protein function in the absence of downregulation.
long-term elevation of monoamine levels can uncouple receptors from G-proteins without downregulating receptors.
chronic monoamine transport inhibition produces a selective and specific reduction in the coupling of monoamine receptors to G-proteins.
